# Resources

## Forum

If you are actively using the package, join the [GeoPressure forum](https://geopressure.discourse.group) to stay informed about bugs, issues, and improvements.

## Main Publications

Main paper presenting the approach to estimate a likelihood map from pressure timeseries:

> Nussbaumer, R., Gravey, M., Briedis, M., & Liechti, F. (2023). Global positioning with animal-borne pressure sensors. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*, 14, 1104–1117. <https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.14043>

Paper presenting the movement model:

> Nussbaumer, R., Gravey, M., Briedis, M., Liechti, F. & Sheldon, D. (2023) Reconstructing bird trajectories from pressure and wind data using a highly optimised hidden Markov model. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*, 14, 1118–1129. <https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.14082>

Paper reviewing the strengths, limitations, and opportunities of geolocation by pressure from a more applied perspective:

> Rhyne, G. S., Stouffer P. C., Briedis, M., Nussbaumer, R. (2024). Barometric geolocators can reveal unprecedented details about the migratory ecology of small birds. *Ornithology*. <https://doi.org/10.1093/ornithology/ukae010>

> Raphaël Nussbaumer, Colin Jackson, Lennox Kirao, Felix Liechti. The potential of multi-sensor geolocators to study short-distance Afrotropical migrants. November 2022. *15th Pan-African Ornithological Congress*. PRESENTATION available as [PDF](http://dx.doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.28757.50408).

## Use with an AI assistant

An AI assistant can guide you through a GeoPressureR analysis, answer questions about the code and
the method, and help you share or reuse data. The **geopressure** skill, from
[GeoPressureSkills](https://github.com/GeoPressure/GeoPressureSkills), tells the assistant where
each kind of answer lives (this manual, the function reference, the papers, the forum) and how to
work with you.

- **Claude Code** (the command-line tool, or the Code tab of the Claude desktop app) can run R on
  your computer, so it can set up a GeoPressureTemplate project and run the analysis with you:

  ```
  /plugin marketplace add GeoPressure/GeoPressureSkills
  /plugin install geopressure@geopressure
  ```

- **Claude.ai or the Claude desktop chat:** download `geopressure.zip` from the
  [latest release](https://github.com/GeoPressure/GeoPressureSkills/releases/latest) and upload it
  at [claude.ai/customize/skills](https://claude.ai/customize/skills) (**+**, **Create skill**,
  **Upload a skill**). Without R, the assistant answers questions and writes scripts for you to run.
- **Other assistants** that read skills: copy the `plugins/geopressure/skills/geopressure` folder
  to the folder your assistant reads skills from.

Projects created from GeoPressureTemplate also include an `AGENTS.md` file, which guides any
assistant through the analysis, with or without the skill.

You stay in charge of the judgement calls: the assistant prepares and checks, but you label the
flights in `trainset()` and decide on the settings. Check its results as you would a colleague's,
and never paste a key or password into the chat (see below).

## Accounts and keys

Most of a GeoPressureR analysis needs no account. Pressure maps and ERA5 time series are computed
through the GeoPressure API, which is free and needs no key. A few steps need your own account:

| Account | Needed for | Required? |
|---|---|---|
| [Copernicus Climate Data Store](https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu) (ECMWF) | Downloading wind with `tag_download_wind()`. When a key is stored, `geopressure_timeseries()` and `pressurepath_create()` also read ERA5 from ECMWF's ARCO service instead of the GeoPressure API (see their `source` argument). | Only for wind |
| [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org) | Publishing a GeoLocator Data Package, and checking a draft with `GeoLocatoR::read_zenodo(draft = TRUE)` | Only to publish |
| [GitHub](https://github.com) | Creating a project with "Use this template" and archiving your code on Zenodo. `GeoLocatoR::create_geopressuretemplate()` needs git installed, but no account. | Optional |
| CARTO, Mapbox, MapTiler | More basemap styles in the interactive maps | Optional |

Keys are personal. Store each one once in your system keyring, as shown below, so that it never
appears in a script, in `config.yml` or in a repository. Do not paste a key into a chat or share it
with an AI assistant: run the commands yourself. `keyring::key_list()` lists the stored services
without showing the keys.

### Copernicus Climate Data Store

1. Create an ECMWF account on the [Climate Data Store](https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu).
2. Accept the "Licence to use Copernicus Products" in the
   [Licences tab of the ERA5 pressure levels dataset](https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/datasets/reanalysis-era5-pressure-levels?tab=download#manage-licences).
   Requests fail until the licence is accepted.
3. Copy your Personal Access Token from your [profile page](https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/profile).
4. Store it with `ecmwfr`, which calls it a key:

```{r accounts-cds-key}
#| eval: false
ecmwfr::wf_set_key("<your personal access token>")
```

GeoPressureR then finds the key by itself. The CDS limits how many requests each account can have
queued; see [Trajectory with wind](trajectory-with-wind.html) for downloading wind.

### Zenodo

1. Create a [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org) account. You can sign in with ORCID or GitHub.
2. Create a personal access token in your
   [Zenodo token settings](https://zenodo.org/account/settings/applications/tokens/new/).
3. Store it in the keyring. `key_set()` asks for the token, so it is not saved in your R history:

```{r accounts-zenodo-token}
#| eval: false
keyring::key_set("ZENODO_TOKEN")
```

`read_zenodo()` also reads the token from a `ZENODO_TOKEN` environment variable. See
[Publish your data](geolocator-create.html) for the publishing steps.

### Map tiles

Interactive GeoPressureR maps use a basemap to provide geographic context. GeoPressureViz,
GeoLightViz, `plot()` maps, and `plot_path()` all show the same basemap selector.

Esri's Gray Canvas, imagery, and topographic basemaps are always available. You can add CARTO,
Mapbox, or MapTiler styles by storing a provider key once in your system keyring.

```{r map-tiles-keyring}
#| eval: false
keyring::key_set_with_value("CARTO_API_KEY", password = "<your CARTO API key>")
keyring::key_set_with_value("MAPBOX_ACCESS_TOKEN", password = "<your Mapbox token>")
keyring::key_set_with_value("MAPTILER_API_KEY", password = "<your MapTiler API key>")
```

Only store a public, read-only Mapbox token: rendered Leaflet maps send map tokens to the web
browser. Do not put keys in analysis scripts or commit them to version control. Create keys at
[CARTO](https://carto.com/basemaps/apikey/),
[Mapbox](https://docs.mapbox.com/help/getting-started/access-tokens/), or
[MapTiler](https://www.maptiler.com/cloud/).

Each configured provider adds useful styles to the selector: CARTO Dark Matter with and without
labels; Mapbox Dark, Outdoors, Satellite, and Satellite Streets; and MapTiler DataViz Dark,
Topographic, Satellite, and Hybrid. Choose a dark no-label layer for likelihood maps, a
topographic layer for terrain context, and satellite or hybrid imagery for local detail.
